# Preface.

Without deciding here whether <term>Freemasonry</term> <note>a fraternal organization that evolved from medieval stonemasons' guilds into a system of morality and philosophy</note> is truly connected with magic, <term>theurgy</term> <note>a form of ritual magic intended to invoke divine or supernatural powers</note>, and <term>Kabbalah</term> <note>an ancient Jewish tradition of mystical interpretation of the Bible</note>, the interest that Freemasons and <term>Rosicrucians</term> <note>members of a secret society claiming to possess esoteric wisdom passed down from antiquity</note> take in one another is well known. The writings emerging from both branches are always interesting, even if discord reigns among the <term>systems</term> <note>the various organizational structures, rites, and degrees of Masonry, which often disagreed on their origins and purposes</note> of their authors. However, it is precisely this diversity of systems that makes it so difficult to find common ground of general interest. For this reason, it is believed that a collection of scholarly and historical essays—intended for all systems and branches of Freemasonry—which contains significant material from old and new works, impartially announces and judges all recent writings, and subsequently recounts the latest events faithfully, would surely find approval and support.

<summary>This preface introduces a collection of essays intended to bridge the various branches and systems of Freemasonry and Rosicrucianism by focusing on historical and scholarly interests rather than sectarian disputes.</summary>
<keywords>Freemasonry, Rosicrucianism, Theurgy, Kabbalah, Secret Societies, Masonic Systems, Periodicals, Esotericism</keywords>

<sig>I.</sig>

# Preface.

This is the intention of the editor of this <term>Archive</term> <note>referring to the publication itself, which serves as a repository for documents and essays</note>, though only in part; it cannot be fully explained here, nor can it be judged based on a single installment. One can only remark that its continuation alone will and can provide perfection and completeness.

In order to achieve this more and more, we request, on the one hand, suggestions for improvement according to the taste of discerning readers; and on the other, reports of new and remarkable occurrences in <term>Masonry</term> <note>original: "Maurerei"</note>, both public and private; biographies or materials for such concerning notable men; interesting anecdotes; and new <term>Masonic</term> and <term>Rosicrucian</term> writings; sent to the address of the publisher.

It is noted here that in the future, we will primarily work toward providing a productive <term>critique</term> <note>original: "Kritik"; here meaning a scholarly review or analytical evaluation</note> of everything that has been written in older and newer times regarding the subjects pertaining to this field. Furthermore, new essays will also appear, which we flatter ourselves will attract attention and be pleasing to most readers.

### I.

## What is a Freemason?

If someone were presented with the questions: What is a legal scholar? <term>an advocate</term> <note>original: "Sachwalter"; a representative in legal matters, similar to an attorney</note>? a physician? a philosopher? then in the answer one would certainly expect to know how all these men, in their individual circumstances, differ from all other scholars and <term>estates</term> <note>original: "Stände"; referring to the social classes or professional ranks that defined 18th-century social structure</note>; yet the questioner's intention is likely primarily this: that one makes known to him the essential purpose of the profession, the essential quality of the man, so that he may, when the occasion arises, test his people, and not remain in uncertainty whether the man who presents himself as a member of one of the named estates is truly what he claims to be, or whether he has only adopted the name, while possessing hardly even the most insignificant of the essential qualities.

Thus, for example, someone can [receive] from a philosophical faculty the diploma of a Doctor of World- <note>The word is cut off here by the page break; the catchword indicates it completes as "World-wisdom" (Weltweisheit), a common 18th-century term for philosophy</note>

wisdom and the title of Master of the Seven Liberal Arts, or have been enrolled among the doctors by the law faculty of a university (like the well-known, unfortunate Doctor of Laws, **William Dodd** <note>William Dodd (1729–1777) was an English clergyman and man of letters who was famously executed for forgery. Though he held a doctorate in laws, he was primarily known as a "Macaroni Parson" or celebrity preacher.</note>, who was actually a theologian), and yet, for all that, be neither a philosopher nor a legal scholar. On the other hand, there lives here and there, in some solitary seat, many a man whom his age does not know, who is mentioned neither in the address books, nor in **Meusel’s Lexicon of Scholars** <note>Johann Georg Meusel was a famous 18th-century bibliographer; his "Gelehrtes Teutschland" was the standard biographical dictionary of German writers of the time.</note>, nor in the libraries of the nitpickers, and who nevertheless unites within himself the knowledge of all <term>forty</term> <note>original: "Quarante"; a reference to the forty members of the Académie Française, often called "the immortals."</note> members of an academy in his own person; and just as Mercury in the works of **Plautus** <note>original: "Merkur beim Plautus"; a reference to the Roman play *Amphitryon*, where the god Mercury takes on the appearance of a servant and boasts of his prowess.</note> struck for four men, he is as learned as forty academicians, to whom, taken together, **Piron** <note>Alexis Piron (1689–1773) was a French epigrammatist and wit known for his biting sarcasm directed at the French Academy.</note> would not even grant the erudition of four other honest men.

One finds this truth nowhere so strongly confirmed as in **Freemasonry**. We Freemasons ourselves must admit that of the twenty thousand brothers who may live and move in Germany (an exact calculation and list is impossible for many reasons), hardly twenty are true Masons.

There is, therefore, a considerable difference between Masons in general and true Masons. It is the same difference that prevails between Masters of Philosophy and philosophers, between Doctors of Medicine and physicians, between apothecaries and <term>chemists</term> <note>original: "Scheidekünstler"; literally "separation artists," a historical term for chemists who specialized in the analysis and decomposition of substances.</note>. ...as it is usually spoken of in the **profane world** <note>original: "profanen Welt"; the world outside of the Masonic lodge, i.e., the uninitiated.</note>, to discover who is a Freemason—that is, who is admitted into lodges and other assemblies of brothers—so difficult is it, by contrast, for the brothers themselves to encounter a true Mason.

---

The question is therefore not at all insignificant: what is a Freemason? It amounts to this: what is a true Mason, and by what shall one distinguish the few genuine ones from the infinitely many ungenuine?

Some brothers, who are enthusiastically prejudiced in favor of a cause they do not know and do not deserve to know, will indeed be ready with an answer. They will say: "Only those who belong to our **system** <note>In 18th-century Masonry, a "system" refers to a specific Rite or organizational structure, such as the *Strict Observance* or the *Zinnendorf Rite*, which often claimed exclusive legitimacy.</note>, which alone is **orthodox** <note>original: "orthodox"; here used to mean "correct" or "officially sanctioned" doctrine.</note>, are genuine; all others are false, ungenuine, and contemptible. They may not set foot in our lodge, and can expect from us hardly any general love of humanity, much less that tender affection with which one brother should embrace another." One must let such **bubbling heads** <note>original: "ſprudelnde Köpfe"; impulsive, over-excited, or "effervescent" individuals.</note> fizzle out; in the end they will perhaps—or perhaps not, though both to their own detriment—become wise. Usually they have hardly any concept of connection, system, **membership roll** <term>Matrikel</term> <note>A formal register or list of members belonging to a lodge or order.</note>, and **installation** <note>The formal ceremony of inducting a Mason into an office or degree.</note>; or their entire knowledge is limited to the outward form, leaves the materials untouched, and their understanding has not penetrated a hair's breadth <note>original: "keine Linie breit"; literally "not a line's width."</note> into the interior of this sublime subject.

Whoever [is part] of the number of members prescribed for a lodge of the degree he possesses, in [one] with the...

...indicates a Lodge provided with a **Constitution** <note>A formal charter or founding document granted by a Grand Lodge or higher Masonic authority.</note> from a higher authority, is called, in the ordinary sense, a free and accepted **Mason** <term>Maurer</term>.

Let us pause here for a while. Since examples and parables are such good means of explanation, we shall resort to one again. A man may care to hold a title out of ambition, or perhaps to make it easier to win a wife, and so forth. His **sovereign lord** <note>original: "Landesherr"; the local prince or ruler of a German state.</note> grants it to him upon his humble petition in exchange for ready cash. Through this, he now obtains all sorts of advantages—all, or at least some, of those he desired. Yet these open no further prospects to him; even if his purchased status suggests the possession of his prince's secrets, he does not come a single step closer to the prince's confidence. His expectation would have been foolish had he anticipated a right to be employed in state business, or even a kind of obligation from the lord toward him. At the very least, he must wait until time and circumstances align so that the prince's choice falls upon him, though he has now secured the possibility that it might fall upon him when the occasion arises.

Precisely this is the case with common **Freemasons** <term>Freimäurer</term>. How greatly do the **uninitiated** <note>original: "Laien"; literally "laity." In this context, it refers to those outside the craft (profane) or those who have joined but lack deeper understanding.</note> err in their opinion when they believe that as soon as they have paid the **initiation fees** <note>original: "Eintrittsgelder"; fees paid upon joining a lodge, which the author notes are necessary for the "benevolent secondary purposes" (charity) of the large organization.</note> (which are certainly necessary for an **institution** <term>Institut</term> so extensive and dedicated to such benevolent secondary purposes), they then possess all the secrets that one is meant to work through...

<summary>The author uses a parable about buying a noble title to explain that joining a lodge and paying fees only makes one a Mason "in name," without granting automatic access to deeper wisdom or the "prince's confidence."</summary>

...indicates, will unfold before them and open the gates of the **sanctuary** <term>Heiligthum</term> <note>In a Masonic context, this refers to the inner chamber or "Holy of Holies," symbolizing deeper spiritual knowledge.</note> to them. For often it would be absolutely impossible for those who pressed the seal of **consecration** <term>Weihung</term> upon their foreheads to satisfy this longing, since it remains unsatisfied even within themselves.

Granting for a moment the possibility of a truly important **secret** <term>Geheimnis</term> in **Masonry** <term>Maurerei</term>—and that is perhaps the least one can demand—but considering on the other hand that even without such a secret—that is to say, even if **Brother A** or **Brother Z**, and nineteen thousand nine hundred and seventy or eighty out of the imagined twenty thousand German Masons, were never to have anything of the secret discovered or entrusted to them except perhaps from the furthest distance—that even without this, Masonry carries with it many **realities** <term>Realitäten</term> for every thinking mind, and manifold pleasure for every man of feeling: yet it is no unreasonable demand to establish that even the common Mason, as a Mason, should *be something*, distinguished from ordinary men by certain qualities and merits.

When the world reads a great portion of the latest **Masonic writings** <term>maurerischen Schriften</term>, it must be striking to the thoughtful reader that everyone who knows the matter, or pretends to know it, makes such an important distinction between the **true** and the **ordinary** Masons, and that the value of those who (in their parlance) are not yet **perfected** <note>original: "vollendet"; this likely refers to Masons who have not yet attained the higher degrees or "High Grades" of the system being discussed.</note> is so humiliatingly disparaged.

<summary>The author argues that even if the "true secrets" of Freemasonry are only known to a tiny fraction of its members, the craft should still provide moral and intellectual value to the average member. He notes a growing and disparaging divide in Masonic literature between the "true" initiated elite and the "ordinary" rank-and-file members.</summary>

One might with good reason suspect a dishonest cause, harmful to the **Order** <term>Orden</term> <note>In this context, the "Order" refers to the organizational body of Freemasonry.</note> itself, for such expressions, were it not that various reasons—and **impartiality** <term>Unpartheilichkeit</term> itself—could convince us not only of the possibility, but of the actual existence of a **true Masonry** <term>Maurerei</term> (taken in the most exalted sense of the word).

The adventurous tales which brothers of reputation, insight, and honesty tell regarding the appearance of a "true Mason," and through which they—contrary to their good intentions—give rise to so many deceptions, are the reason why in the course of this **treatise** <term>Abhandlung</term> several unmistakable, essential characteristics of a true Mason will be provided. Such a figure is truly a most rare **moral phenomenon** <term>Phänomen</term>. Thus, sincere or simple-hearted brothers shall be warned to close their ears to the **charlatan** <term>Scharlatan</term> <note>A common concern in 18th-century Masonry was the "charlatan"—imposters who claimed to possess high-degree secrets or alchemical powers to swindle members.</note>; conversely, they should open their full confidence only to the Mason recognized as authentic according to those signs.

The high degree of improbability—which possesses almost the value of a morally negative certainty—facing so many honest and insightful men living in the bosom of Masonry (namely the ratio of one in a thousand chance of penetrating to the light <note>original: "zum Licht zu dringen"; a central metaphor in Freemasonry for attaining true spiritual or intellectual enlightenment.</note>), would indeed be detrimental to the whole of an institution that is estimable in so many respects. Therefore, to reassure these brothers, we wish first only to describe the common **Freemason** <term>Freimaurer</term>; and even if we perhaps do not describe him quite as...

> “Forgive me, worthy Masonic brothers, for what my love for you has caused me to say thus far. Forgive me, you noble, great men who are my brothers, to whom my heart is attached. Oh! I did not wish to offend you; my heart would be torn asunder if it had offended you. But what have I said that the wiser Mason must not have felt just as well as I? Only to say it, to say it publicly, he did not dare. My duty—for I consider what I have done to be my duty—commanded me to speak while you remain silent. *) Let us take the matter as it stands. Let us extract the excellent principles, even if other reasons might give them a different purpose. Let not the art with which our **Scots** <term>Schotten</term> <note>original: "Schotten"; refers to the "Scottish Rite" or high-degree Masonry, which was often criticized by reformers for being overly preoccupied with complex rituals and titles.</note> torment themselves be the goal of our endeavors. Masonry shows us a nobler, more beneficial art: the art of forming good human beings <note>original: "Menschenbildung"; a central Enlightenment concept referring to the holistic moral and intellectual cultivation of a person.</note>.”

<page-num>8</page-num>

So, assuming the Order has no secret—at least no secret for the majority of the brothers—there nevertheless remain many essential advantages.

> “And why should we not seek good people where they are surely to be found; train them where Nature has provided all the foundations? Why should we not take Masons on a new footing from exactly those places, and expect them from those very directions toward which the gates of our Temple are opened? From North and South, from West and East?”

It is strange that the same period in which the **Knights Templar** <term>Tempelherren</term> <note>A medieval military order; many Masonic myths link the origins of the Lodge to the Templars' survival after their suppression in 1312.</note> made themselves known, which produced the Masons and gave rise to the **Knights of St. John** <term>Johannesrittern</term> <note>Also known as the Hospitallers; another medieval order of knights often cited in the legendary histories of Masonic degrees.</note>, did not have the same influence on all other associations as it did on **Masonry** <term>Maurerei</term>. While all other orders restricted themselves to the orthodox Christian, the Masonic Order, by contrast, permitted entry to every honest man of every faith and every station. To be sure, if it is true that a reform of the Order according to the then-emerging Christian system was actually undertaken in the seventh century, then some **Lodges** <term>Logen</term> certainly have a point when they exclude from their **secret** <term>Geheimniß</term> anyone who will not swear by this newer revelation <note>The "newer revelation" refers to the New Testament and the Christian faith.</note>. And yet, that is not the teaching of the higher Order; on the contrary, a traveling **Scot** <term>Schott</term> <note>Refers to a member of the "Scottish Rite," a series of "higher" degrees in Freemasonry that claimed more ancient or profound knowledge than the basic three degrees.</note> of great authority actually found fellow guild members even in Fez and Morocco whose faith was the teaching of **Muhammad** <term>Muhammed</term> <note>In the 18th century, stories of "Moorish" or "Oriental" Masons were often used to illustrate the Enlightenment ideal that morality and brotherhood are universal and not exclusive to Christianity.</note>, as it is said to have manifested itself even in their rituals. The Order could thus become a tool to unite upright men of all nations and to tie the universal **bond of brotherhood** <term>Bruderband</term> between people more tightly. But how futile is perhaps this hope, which...

“...[that which] I dared to grasp in a seductive dream: to restore through **Freemasonry** <term>Freimaurerei</term> the true **Temple of Nature** <note>An Enlightenment-era concept referring to a universal, rational religion based on natural law and virtue rather than specific sectarian dogmas.</note>, into whose secrets every upright person would be initiated, and whose priest every friend of God and his kind <note>The original term "Gattung" refers to the human species or humankind.</note> would be! How could **intolerance** <term>Unduldsamkeit</term> extend even into these remote dwellings and deny participation in the alleged advantages to all non-Christians! It is to the credit of the **Dutch lodges** <note>Dutch Freemasonry was famously more inclusive than its German counterparts in the 18th century, particularly regarding the admission of Jewish members.</note> that they (to the offense of others) admit **Jews**.”

“It may seem impractical to some here when they see this promotion of **tolerance** <term>Toleranz</term> recommended as one of the works of the Order. However, it is not only highly worthy of the **Masonic institution** <term>Freimaurerinstituts</term> but also accords very well with a part of its activities. I do not mean to say that one should teach specific religious opinions; on the contrary, I would vote entirely against that. Rather, one should highlight and praise the good from every church or religion, and while not violently opposing that which could lead to excesses <note>Likely referring to religious fanaticism, superstition, or sectarian conflict.</note>, gradually suppress it, weaken the impression it can make on the mind, and in such a way unite the peoples—to transplant among all nations the sentiment of **brotherly love** <term>Bruderliebe</term>, and what would now be one and the same, the **love of humanity** <term>Menschenliebe</term>: Freemasons, what a task! How honorable for him who completes it! How easy for you, who belong to all classes, and can therefore influence all classes.”

It specifically highlights the inclusion of Jewish members in Dutch lodges as a model for overcoming religious intolerance.</summary>

> “Why should the human race not be able to return to its original rights? Why should the true **Golden Age** <note>A reference to the mythical "Golden Age" of antiquity, a time of peace and primordial innocence often used by Enlightenment thinkers to describe a future state of perfected reason.</note> not visit mortals? — Our more highly developed mental faculties cannot possibly have suppressed innocence and peace with oneself, and all-encompassing love for everyone within man; they cannot have made him incapable of it. Were it so, I would be the first to renounce my current claims on society in order to once again assert the claims of humanity. But it is not so. The feeling for others is not stifled in our senses; it only needs igniting sparks to break out into full flame again. Oh! May this time not be far off! May this **Temple of Nature** <term>Tempel der Natur</term> soon be erected; may the fathers soon see the light and soon cast off the veil that delusion, self-interest, and habit had drawn before their eyes! May the good people of every land be the voluntary **Masons** <term>Maurer</term> who return to Nature her **sanctuary** <term>Heiligthum</term>, from which she was violently displaced.”

My first means would be this: to move the **clergy** <term>Geistlichen</term> themselves to [take part] in the labors, indirectly or directly, as members or as frien[ds]—”

The author uses evocative, almost alchemical imagery here to mock the pretensions of those who claim divine illumination.</note> Certainly, some *visionaries* <term>Schwärmer</term> <note>In the 18th century, "Schwärmer" was a derogatory term for those who claimed direct, irrational divine inspiration or pursued the occult.</note> would very much like to persuade us of this; but when has a true *Mason* <term>Maurer</term> ever spoken in such a way? He cannot do so, because otherwise a very striking contradiction would be revealed within the individual arrangements of *Masonry* <term>Maurerei</term>.

For either the *Superiors of the system* <note>The "Obern" refers to the high-ranking leaders or "Unknown Superiors" claimed by certain mystical Masonic rites of the time, such as the Strict Observance.</note> have already reached the goal of *supernatural knowledge*, or are at least on the right path toward it; or they are still seeking that exclusively correct path. If the latter were the case, it would be as if a blind man were to entrust himself to a man no less blind. And if the former were true, every *impartial observer* <term>Unpartheiische</term> would have to recognize that the means chosen for the cultivation <term>Kultivirung</term> of those types of knowledge and powers are highly impractical; because the loud, noisy external arrangements, connected with so many distractions, would completely divert the spirit from its speculations. Furthermore, instead of a pious elevation toward God—of which so much boast is made in some places—these things would fill the heart with coldness and indifference through too many, and in part immoral, matters.

Fourthly, one cannot let it go unnoticed that many a scientific and artistic talent has found education and support through the **Order**.

We do not wish to take into account here various secondary benefits which, in addition to the primary benefits indicated earlier, arise for a member from his connection. Anyone to whom nature has granted sharp wit and a feeling for the truth will already feel and experience the animating spirit of the whole while at the apprentice level <note>original: "Lehrlingsstufe" — the first degree of Freemasonry.</note>. In general, the study of <term>Masonry</term> <note>original: "Maurerei" — shorthand for Freemasonry.</note> has become a very strange matter. Whoever prefers to imagine the moon as a light that serves to illuminate one hemisphere of the earth at certain times has—imperfect as this concept is—still a more correct idea than a **St. Petersburg fool** <note>original: "Petersburger Thor" — "Thor" is an archaic German word for a fool. Finally, the **negative study** of Masonry can also have a very positive benefit; for, assuming a few positive attributes of an essence, even negations <note>original: "Negationen" — the act of defining something by what it is not.</note> will acquire the value of affirmative definitions. The tree in my garden that bears no fruit, whose blossoms give no scent, and which has no leaves in winter, is no apple tree, no fir, and no linden, but most likely an oak—though it could just as well be an ash or a birch.

# Second Section.
## On Magic and its Kinds.

A quite famous legal scholar <note>Andrea Alciato (1492–1550), an Italian jurist whose book *Emblemata* created a massive craze for "emblems"—pictures combined with moral poems.</note> *) has taken the opportunity in his emblems to represent the three causes of ignorance through the image of the **Sphinx**: specifically, **lust** by its face, **inconstancy** <note>Meaning a lack of steadiness or reliability in one's character.</note> by its wings, and **pride** by its feet. I believe one could make this depiction even more complete by also illustrating the *effect* of ignorance through the cruelty of that monster, who found pleasure in casting all those who could not or would not solve its riddle down from its rock. For in the same way, ignorance has, at all times, exerted every possible effort to at least ruin and undermine the credit and good name of all those who—because more worthy occupations were open to them—did not wish to occupy themselves with its follies and childishness.

## Fourth Section.
### That the great learning of many upright men has often been interpreted as magic.

A farmer named Furius Chresimus <note>original: "Furius Krisinius"; this refers to Gaius Furius Chresimus, a freedman mentioned by the Roman author Pliny the Elder in his "Natural History."</note> was accused by the Roman people because he had allegedly placed enchanting stones on the fields of his neighbors, which—though they were larger and much more extensive—nevertheless did not yield as good a harvest as his own. To justify his innocence, he wished to use no other means to prove it than to show himself on the appointed day with all the tools necessary for agriculture, all of which were in the best condition. He asked the judges only to believe that he had used no other poison or illicit means than the use of these tools through tireless labor, and persistent wakefulness and diligence—which, to his great displeasure, he could not present to them at the same time as his tools. # Section Five.

## That Mathematics has Placed Many Mathematicians Under the Suspicion of Magic.

Among all the sound rules that can serve to guide and direct our actions, it seems to me, with good reason, that none is more useful or correct than that which teaches us that poison is usually administered only in sweet syrups, and vice is accustomed to deceive only under the guise of virtue. For we truly see every day in our experience that just as counterfeiters lay a few leaves of gold or silver over their base coins to circulate them among the people as good and valid currency: so too the majority of people, who would never be sought out for the sake of the value of their scholarship, find themselves forced to hide and assume another name. 

Thus, the heretics are called **theologians**, the "fire-dabblers" <term>Fire-dabblers: Translated from "Feuersudler," a derogatory term for clumsy or unscientific alchemists who obsessed over their furnaces without true theory.</term> are called **chemists**, the charlatans are called **physicians**, the sophists are called **philosophers**, and the sorcerers are called **Mathematici** <note>original: "Mathematici" – in the early modern period, this Latin term was used broadly to include mathematicians, astronomers, and astrologers; because of the latter, the term often carried a connotation of fortune-telling or occultism.</note>. 

This has now created such confusion among things, and especially among the sciences, that even if it is not impossible, one must still admit it is very difficult to distinguish the true teachers of these branches of knowledge from the ignorant and the reckless daredevils who also involve themselves with them. Because these men have tossed these sciences together with an infinite multitude of deceitful and superstitious things, they have made them so suspicious that

Just as the common folk <term>Pöbel<note>A term used here to describe the uneducated masses of the medieval period.</note></term> consider those to be sorcerers <note>original: "Zauberer"</note> who display roses and other spring flowers in the depths of winter: so all those excellent men, who appear as shining stars in the middle of this dark night, and who produced such admirable fruits of their erudition <note>original: "Gelehrsamkeit"</note> for the sciences during the harshest of seasons, have been passed down to us under the names given to them by the ignorance and credulity <note>original: "Leichtgläubigkeit"</note> of their contemporaries. The empty and powerless spirits of those people bowed all the more easily under the weight of a false persuasion—a companion of ignorance that follows at its heels just as surely as a shadow follows a body or envy follows virtue.

We can derive from this the fourth cause of this suspicion held against so many great men. It consists, namely, in an excessive credulity regarding deceitful and superstitious things, which usually follow one after another. ## Section Ten.
### Defense of Pythagoras.

**I**f Plutarch \*) <note>Plutarch (c. 46 – 119 AD), a Greek philosopher and biographer</note> did not inform us about Pythagoras that he had the habit of freely and frankly confessing that the greatest advantage he ever drew from philosophy consisted in the fact that he was no longer surprised by anything in the world: I would hardly be able to convince myself that he would not presently fall into the greatest astonishment, were he to witness how the malice and ignorance of men have so distorted the truth of his history and the real sense of his teaching that his life looks like the adventures of a charlatan and a juggler <note>original: *Taschenspieler*, literally "pocket-player," referring to a sleight-of-hand magician or street performer</note>, and his principles appear fabulous, foolish, and completely groundless. Indeed, this science was necessary to him, which is why he pursued it almost passionately; for example, he was delighted with joy when he had discovered the theorem named after him, <note>The Pythagorean Theorem ($a^2 + b^2 = c^2$), which describes the relationship between the sides of a right-angled triangle.</note>

# III.

## Defense of Higher Chemistry.

->(From the chemical lectures of the eminent Hermann Boerhaave <note>Hermann Boerhaave (1668–1738) was a Dutch physician and chemist. His teaching at the University of Leiden was so influential that he is often called the "teacher of Europe."</note>.)<-

---

### §. 1.

### Introduction to what higher chemistry actually achieves in general.

It is solely through chemistry that it first became known to us that in every single body, be it <term>animal or vegetable</term> <note>At this time, "animal" and "vegetable" were two of the three primary kingdoms of nature (the third being mineral).</note>, there dwells a certain <term>spirit</term> <note>original: "Geist." In 18th-century chemistry, this refers to a "spiritus rector" or a volatile essence that contains the unique properties—especially the scent—of a substance.</note> peculiar to every physical being, which is so fine that it reveals itself only through smell and taste or through its own particular effects. This <term>vapor</term> <note>original: "Dunst."</note> of the body represents its complete essence so entirely that it is the primary means by which one distinguishes one thing precisely from another. It is, however, so delicate that it cannot be seen even through a magnifying glass nor grasped or felt with the hands, and at the same time, it is highly volatile. As soon as it is pure and free on its own, it does not rest, but flies away with a constant mobility, mixes with the air, and thus passes into the general <term>chaos</term> <note>In the context of Boerhaave’s chemistry, "chaos" refers to the atmosphere, which was seen as a vast, shifting collection of all the volatile spirits and vapors rising from the earth.</note> of all volatile bodies. ### §. 3.

### Influence specifically on Medicine.

Who would dispute the influence on **medicine** <note>original: "Medicin"</note> of a science that is beneficial to the entire study of nature? For medicine concerns itself only with the human body and other bodies, insofar as the latter have an influence on the former. But no one can rightly understand either if they do not call upon **chemistry** <note>original: "Chemie"</note> for help. I do not intend to lay this all out in a strictly systematic order here. 

Only chemistry has shown us that nothing but earthly **foundational parts** <note>original: "Grundtheile"; referring to the elemental or mineral building blocks of matter.</note> constitute the solid matter in our bodies; these are held together by an **oily-fatty glue** <note>original: "öhlichtfetten Leim"; an early chemical term for the organic substances, like lipids or proteins, that bind tissues together.</note> which can only be separated from them by the strongest fire. Chemistry has also taught us that even the water placed between these parts acts as a bond, which is condensed along with the dense parts and, after this condensation, is difficult to drive out from them.

Now, even assuming it is granted that chemistry is useful in **physiology** and **pathology**, most people will still think that it can serve no purpose in **semiotic observations** <term>Semiotics: In a historical medical context, this refers to "semiotics" or "semiology"—the study of the signs and symptoms of diseases.</term>, which the ancient Greeks carried to such great lengths. ### §. 4.

## Influence of Chemistry on the other arts, or on the hand-crafts in particular; where the dyeing arts are considered first.

**Mechanical arts** is the name given to those hand-crafts performed by hand; they are entirely different from that **Mechanics** which mathematicians explain through the common properties of all physical bodies. This latter field gains no advantage from chemistry, but the former do, as they concern themselves with the transformation of bodies through their treatment.

Related to painting is the **art of dyeing** <term>Färbekunst: the craft of applying permanent colors to textiles through chemical reactions</term>, which applies the most delicate colors to silk, cotton, linen, and wool, and prepares garments, ribbons, and the like. This art rests on three parts. First, it must make the surface of the material to be dyed absorbent, so that when it is purely cleaned, it may receive and retain the colors; this is achieved by washing with all kinds of lyes, by soaking, and by pounding. It is known that primarily fermented urine <note>A common historical source of ammonia used to cleanse and prep fabrics</note>, sharp alkali salt <note>original: *Laugensalz*; likely potash or soda ash</note>, all sorts of soaps, and animal gall <note>Ox gall was frequently used as a surfactant to help dyes penetrate fibers</note> accomplish this. The oily, fatty impurities of the wool and the fatty, tough dirt of the linen are likewise washed out. In the preparation, selection, and application of all these means, the science of an uncommon **chemist** achieves much and constantly adds new, useful inventions to the old. The second part belonging here is the proper mixing of colors, in order to unite them exactly with the previously prepared body, so that they constantly retain their fresh luster and appearance. In this matter, **chemistry** has shown what it can do.

It is no wonder, for the blue copper color, the violet, and the green of copper can be presented at the artist's whim—dark or light, in such a charming variety—that they must please. ### §. 5.
## Special Influence on the Arts of Glass and Stones.

The art of glassmaking is useful to the human race above many others. Through it and **glass-grinding** <note>the process of shaping and polishing glass to create lenses for spectacles or telescopes</note>, one comes to the aid of the defects of sight. If one were to take it away, how would an elderly person ever manage their scholarly pursuits? We have it to thank that, while secured against heat and frost and protected from filth, we can still see everything clearly through it; thus, even the wind cannot hinder us, whether we sit quietly at home or travel in coaches and ships. Pure glass, which is not easily corrupted by foreign substances, can be easily cleaned again if it becomes soiled. What is kept inside it can be seen constantly, without the contents being changed by it, nor the glass itself being easily altered. Whatever has been preserved in a glass sealed on all sides remains unspoiled and unchanged. Even the <term>Alkahest</term> <note>A hypothetical "universal solvent" sought by alchemists, which was believed to be capable of dissolving any substance, including gold, into its primary liquid form</note> itself—if such a thing ever existed—cannot affect glass, which no corrosive substances can harm; whether it boils within, or through

### §. 6.
## Metallurgy.

The art of metals depends so entirely upon chemistry that it seems to have made chemistry quite particularly its own. I do not yet mean here that art which boasts of the creation and transformation <note>This refers to transmutation, the alchemical goal of changing base metals into gold</note> of metals. I will honestly reveal some of my thoughts on that later when I speak of the influence of art on alchemy. But here, one should understand that science which teaches how to make metals suitable for the utility and ornament of mankind.

Gold is often, for various reasons, pale and not properly yellow and shiny, which the chemist then enhances with a <term>cement</term> <note>original: "Cäment"; in this context, a mixture of salts and minerals used in a dry-heat process to purify or color the surface of gold</note> or <term>regulus of antimony</term> <note>original: "Spießglaskönig"; the metallic form of antimony, used in the refining of gold to separate it from other metals</note>; thus, the Dutch ducats <note>High-purity gold coins used throughout Europe for trade</note> struck in the present time have, above all others, a luminous brilliance which the skilled mint-master <note>The official responsible for the quality and production of coins at a mint</note> knows how to give them through his art. This same metal, if it were entirely pure, would be too soft for coinage. Therefore, through a precisely determined addition of copper or silver, it is made suitable for this necessary use. Silver, too, for daily use...

### Influence on the Art of War.

Therefore, these people seemed to possess a superhuman wisdom to those not initiated into these secrets, and it was believed that they had received such wisdom through commerce with spirits and their instruction. For, and this is the most important point here, as long as the world has stood, people have held the belief that there exist both evil and good spirits <term>Geister; in this context, the author refers to non-corporeal entities like angels, demons, or elemental beings</term>. ### § 9.

### Kitchen Chemistry for Cooking and Brewing.

Of all the other arts, none provides for human needs as much as that which teaches us how to keep foodstuffs from spoiling through various preparations, or how to transform them so that human life may be sustained. This is therefore called the **art of cooking**, or the culinary art, and it serves both the healthy and the sick as a form of medicine <note>In the early modern period, food and medicine were closely linked under the theory of "regimen," where the right diet was considered the first line of defense against illness.</note>. Although this art is ancient and as old as mankind itself, it can still be greatly improved through the application of chemistry.

If simply the **acidic spirit of common sea salt** <term>spirit of salt; known today as hydrochloric acid</term> is extracted through the chemist's art <note>Specifically through distillation of salt with clay or vitriol</note> and mixed with a sufficient amount of water, it provides a powerful preservative for meat, fish, and anything else prone to rot. It prevents spoilage, imparts a pleasant taste, and prepares food most suitably for digestion; indeed, it simultaneously resists the putrefying influences of hot weather and the diseases that arise from such heat. For this same reason, it is such an excellent aid for sailors that it is a marvel; for these people are often forced by necessity to consume spoiled water, rotten fish, smelling meat, and rancid bacon for their survival in the heat. Certainly, **Glauber** <note>Johann Rudolf Glauber (1604–1670), a famous German-Dutch alchemist and chemist known for "Glauber's Salt."</note> deserves great credit in this matter, as he wrote his treatises for the consolation of seafarers and the welfare of Germany, along with other...

### §. 10.

## On Alchemy.

Now I have finally reached the point where I can say a few things—brief, yet all the more sincere—concerning the most excellent utility of the art of **alchemy**. I wish to speak frankly about what I have discovered. Among all the **physical writers** <note>In this period, "physics" or "physical writers" referred to natural philosophers who studied the laws of nature and the properties of matter.</note> I have encountered until now, I have met none who have explored the nature of bodies and their transformative power more deeply, or explained it more clearly, than the **alchemists**. 

And so that no one believes I am speaking with bias here—which is not my way at all—I ask only that one read the primary, authentic authors, and not with mere casual attention. Take, for example, <term>Raimund Lullius</term> <note>Ramon Llull (c. 1232–1316) was a Majorcan philosopher. While the historical Llull was likely not an alchemist, a massive body of alchemical literature was attributed to him (known as Pseudo-Lull), which became foundational to Western alchemy.</note> in that book which he titled his *Experiments* <note>original: "Versuche," likely referring to the *Experientia* or *Testamentum*.</note>. Observe the clarity with which he explains the nature of the **animal**, **mineral**, and **vegetable** <note>These represent the "three kingdoms of nature" traditionally studied by alchemists to understand the composition of the world.</note> in their effects, through simple experiments, without any circumlocution and without the false veneer of imagination. And then tell me sincerely: where else in the study of physics can one find anything similar? 

"Through this **demonstration**," he says—referring to that which places before our eyes the bodies **opened** <note>In alchemy, to "open" a body (aufschließen) means to break it down into its constituent parts or essential elements through chemical processes.</note> by our art—"we compel assent infinitely more securely and certainly than through all other grounds of proof." ### The Generation of the Stone.

Nature teaches that one animal begets another; so too, according to the Art, the matter of the stone begets the Stone. ## Utility of the Art and the Effect of the Stone.

Beyond the sum of so many pleasures that the possession of this Stone can and will grant—by removing poverty and enabling charity to enjoy, in rich measure, the joy of having diminished the misery of mortals—it heals all diseases and possesses the strongest power among all possible powers. The assembled sages argued for a long time over this Solonic opinion. Bias, Periander, and Pittacus fully agreed with him; however, the majority voted for Seneca, who demonstrated with compelling reasons that the proposed new distribution of the world would lead to even greater disorder and discord. For the mightier lion would still seize the larger portion, whereas the honest and virtuous people would receive far less. He added that although many considered contagious diseases, plague, famine <term>theure Zeit: Literally "dear time," a common historical idiom for periods of high food prices or scarcity.</term>, and war to be the sharpest scourges with which God could punish the human race, this was not actually the case; rather, the most terrible plague that could be imposed by God would be if slaves were to become wealthy and equal to their masters.

Humans were, according to their destiny—as experience also consistently teaches—to be entirely different in their languages and, like **irrational animals** <note>original: "vernunftlosen Thieren." ...peace is abolished, the great defects that exist in the world are revealed. Therefore, the true stumbling block, which is the cause of all the plagues of our time, is this: that princes, driven by greed, thirst for glory, and arrogance, imagine that their sword has a certain and explicit claim <note>original: *Pfandschilling*, literally "earnest money" or "collateral"; here it refers to a perceived right of ownership or a down payment on conquest</note> on all the lands of those princes who are not as powerful as they.

And this happens solely because, through the ambition of princes, the general peace has been transformed into cruel wars, and with them, virtue and vice—as well as the love and affection of man for his own kind—have been changed into miserable envy and hatred. 

A lion recognizes all other lions as lions; but among humans, it is different. To the Englishman, it seems that a Scot is not a brother—as he is in truth—but a beast of an entirely different species and nature; and so it is for the German toward the Italian, the Spaniard toward the Frenchman, and indeed every nation toward a foreigner. Thus, through the insatiable ambition of the powers of this world, justice is suppressed by force, and the human race, which previously was born— <note>the word cuts off mid-sentence: *gebohren* (born)</note> under good and holy laws...

“You wise and venerable men of Greece,” he said, “one has until now listened to your speeches and opinions with great amazement; you have thereby not only maintained your earned fame but increased it in everyone’s eyes. <meta>This page continues the narrative of the founding of the Rosicrucian Brotherhood. The previous page described how Brother C.R. began the order with only four members and started recording their knowledge in a secret language and a text called "Book M."</meta>

Once these eight brothers had organized and arranged everything to the point that no further special labor was required, and each one possessed a complete treatise <note>original: "Aufsatz"</note> on secret and manifest philosophy, they decided they would no longer remain together. Instead, as they had resolved from the very beginning, they distributed themselves into every country. This was done so that not only could their principles be more sharply scrutinized in secret by the learned, but also so they could inform one another if any observation made in this or that land should lead to an error.

They established the following among themselves:

1) None of them should profess any other business than to heal the sick, and all of this for free.

2) No one should be compelled to wear a specific garment for the sake of the Brotherhood, but should instead dress according to the custom of the country.

3) Every brother should present himself every year on "C. Day" at the House of the Holy Spirit <note>original: "St. Spiritus" — the name given to the Order's headquarters</note> (as the residence founded by Brother C. R. C. had been named), or report the reason for his absence.

4) Every brother should look out for a capable person who could succeed him in the event of his death.

5) The word R. C. shall be their seal, watchword <note>original: "Lösung"</note>, and character.

6) The Brotherhood shall remain secret for one hundred years.

They pledged themselves to one another upon these six articles, and the five brothers set out on their journey. Only Brothers B. and D. remained with Father R. C. for one year. When these too [departed]...

For we are accustomed to thinking of things not in their true form, but rather through an image. And who would blame us? If we are instructed through images in childhood, and if we only reach those higher concepts—about which birth tells us nothing and ordinary education only a little—through them: then it is useful, and it eases the investigation, if we represent to ourselves those two thoughts which the understanding can hardly grasp and the heart captures only with effort—the thoughts of **"Life and Death"**—precisely through images. Indeed, nothing stands in closer connection than life and death. As surely as midday follows the morning, so surely does death follow life! What is now here once was not—what is no longer here once was—everything exists in an unceasing succession: links of a chain, where one always interlocks with the other.

What does this succession give us? The concept of **Time**; and thus, we draw our images for life and death from time itself. Since we are rarely strong enough to envision a whole of significant scope exactly as it is, we begin to divide it—and thus we obtain hours and days, months and years.

One hour displaces the next—how truly death displaces life! <note>The speaker uses the German word "verdrängt," which implies a forceful pushing out or superseding, emphasizing the inevitability of the transition.</note> But we go further: one or more hours, which make up a part of the day, differ noticeably from all others—just so, one segment of life distinguishes itself from all the rest.

When the dawn <note>original: "Morgenröthe"; literally "morning-redness." In German Romantic and Masonic thought, the dawn is a frequent symbol for the beginning of a spiritual or physical journey.</note> breaks forth, then the day begins: when the child is born, his human life commences. The light of the day grows with almost every moment: thus, almost before our eyes, the child's powers develop. All other times of day interlock with one another, like youth and old age, until the day loses itself in the night and earthly life ends in another life, which we do not know.

## Theomagical Anthroposophy.

When I had researched the truth that "man, by his origin, was a branch planted in God," and then found that there must therefore be an everlasting drive from the trunk to the crown: the corruption of the same caused me no small grief, and I was horrified that his fruits do not agree with the root. But when I learned that he had tasted of another tree <note>A reference to the Tree of Knowledge of Good and Evil in the Garden of Eden.</note>, my wonder immediately ceased. Rather, I now made it my first and most important concern to lead him back to his original simplicity <term>Simplicity</term> <note>In this context, "simplicity" (Simplizität) refers to a state of being undivided and pure, free from the "complex" mixtures of material corruption and sin.</note>, and to separate all mixtures of evil and good from him. Yet, through his Fall, the noblest parts of his body were so shattered that he had left the soul no knowledge to provide him healing. To proceed in an orderly fashion, I thought it wise to first investigate its elements, and only then to explore the world itself. With this intention, I observed the fruits of spring. I noticed there a great multitude of plants of the earth, fresh and pleasant in their season. But when I looked back at their origin, they were not the same things as these earthly plants.

I applied this observation to the world and arrived at this conclusion: "That in the beginning, the world was not the sort of being it is now, but was a different kind of seed and matter from which the structure we now inhabit arose." ### 1. On Jesuits.

The author himself was a Jesuit. Late, but finally his eyes were opened; it was noticed, but he escaped their vengeance, fled to America, and is now an officer in the <term>provincial army</term> <note>This likely refers to the Continental Army or local militias during the American Revolutionary War era, given the 1782 publication date.</note>. This publication is not without purpose, as he believes, because even in America <term>emissaries</term> <note>secret agents or representatives sent on a mission</note> are sneaking around, and are said to still be operating in the Palatinate, Bavaria, Switzerland, and several other locations. These are the sources from which he has drawn his information. Even now, they are said to be attempting to win over a very esteemed society for themselves through emissaries—an outcome the author hopes to prevent through this work.

The founder of the Jesuit Order was Loyola, born in Spain in 1491 and raised at court. After a period of confinement in a sickbed, he wished to renounce the world, but first intended to travel to Jerusalem; before doing so, he dedicated his weapons to the Blessed Virgin. He then lived with the utmost austerity and wrote his book, *Spiritual Exercises* <note>original: "geistliche Betrachtungen," referring to the *Exercitia Spiritualia*</note>, which was said to have been inspired by the Blessed Virgin and Christ—to whom he now acted as a mediator—despite the claim that he could neither read nor write <note>Ignatius of Loyola was actually literate, but Enlightenment-era critics often emphasized his "fanaticism" or lack of formal education prior to his religious conversion to frame the order's origins as irrational.</note>. Before his departure for Jerusalem, he received a blessing from the Pope. After his journey, he returned to Barcelona, where he was arrested on account of his fanaticism. Upon his release, he went to Salamanca, suffered the same fate there, and then resolved to go to Paris. Here he intended to study, he

<meta>This page continues the critique of the Jesuit Order’s internal governance and its shift toward centralized, absolute power under its early leaders.</meta>

The oracle <note>original: "oraculum"; here referring to a divine-like decree</note> consisted of a favorable word that a Pope let slip at some point, which they immediately adopted as law for the entire world. Their form of government was despotic. The Pope was considered infallible; he had transferred his power to their General, who thus represented the person of Christ, and subordinates were bound to carry out their orders without any reservation. **Laynez** <note>Diego Laínez (1512–1565), the second Superior General, who is often credited with the organizational and political hardening of the order</note>, at their congregations, had himself granted the arbitrary interpretation of laws, arbitrary authorization, power over life and death, and was even allowed to release subjects from obedience to their princes. This latter point was always a central tenet of the Jesuits. The office of a General lasted for life. Once someone was admitted, he had to remain a Jesuit; conversely, he could be expelled from the order by the General without cause being given. To ensure greater harmony, their classes, years of probation, and surveillance served their purpose, as they acted as spies upon one another. The novices were sometimes locked away to habituate them to solitude and to induce visions. There were even secret Jesuits in all families and social classes; one observed the other, and all had to provide precise reports on everything that could be useful to the order. The General received 177 reports <note>original: "Rapports"</note> annually from every kingdom; he, who was accountable to no one, demanded an account of everything. No one was allowed to accept a prelacy <note>a high-ranking ecclesiastical office, such as a bishopric, which would have removed the member from the General's direct control</note>, so as to remain constantly under the tyranny of the General

->2. Letter on Freemasonry, from an experienced member to a profane <note>In Masonic terminology, a "profane" person is one who has not been initiated into the Order.</note> friend.<-

### Chapter 2. A further introduction to the secrets of the ancient sages, who are known by the name of world-sages and Magi, and to their occupations.

The **Mysteries** <note>In this context, "Mysteries" refers to the hidden rites and secret knowledge of ancient philosophical and religious orders, such as those of the Pythagoreans or the Egyptian priests.</note> were dedicated to the wisdom of all things—specifically in the second degree, which was connected to the first. Both shared a common high priest. Great care was taken in selecting the initiates, and the **profane** <note>The "profane" were the uninitiated or those deemed unworthy of entering the secret society.</note> were closely scrutinized; anyone who proposed a candidate had to vouch for them. The second part of the Mysteries was organized into three classes, followed by a fifth, and concluded with the number seven. Each class had its own order and members who knew how to recognize one another, as well as distinct signs of recognition.

The heads of religion possessed a **triangle** in this manner. The heads of the second type also wore such a triangle (although here it signified the symbol of the highest being, the **primal birth** of all natural things, and the all-consuming essence: **fire**). It was meant to signify that those who wore it were masters of the knowledge of all nature and all its powers and constituent parts. They were called **philosophers** and occupied themselves only with one another, although certain things were also taught publicly to the common people by their members. They also bore the name **Magi**, or **Master-Sages**. <term>World-wisdom</term> <note>original: "Weltweisheit" — an 18th-century German term for secular philosophy or the study of the natural world.</note> and philosophy were both very different. There existed the authentic and the false, the general and the specific; we are speaking here, namely, of **hidden wisdom**.

### Chapter 3. A more detailed explanation of the preceding.

The investigation of creation, natural things, their components, and finally the perfection of all nature was the primary occupation. In the assemblies, the men wore special garments—words and signs of their rank. The **hieroglyphs** of the highest order were distinguished from those of the lesser. Not only natural history, but also the **Kabbalah** <note>original: "Kabbale" — here referring to a tradition of mystical interpretation used to predict the future, common in 18th-century occult circles.</note> could occupy them, often for their entire lives. This latter was intended to teach how to foretell future events. No one kept a secret from the **conscience-superiors** <term>conscience-superiors</term> <note>original: "Gewissensobern" — high-ranking officials within the order to whom members were required to confess their thoughts and deeds to ensure total obedience.</note>.

Every initiate had to first confess, specifically in the temple of the **Demiurge** <note>The "Demiurge" is a figure from ancient philosophy, often viewed as the "artisan" or "craftsman" of the physical world; in these secret societies, he was often represented by a statue or a high-ranking official.</note> built in the shape of a **triangle**, behind whose altar there was space for the **speech-machine** and the **machine of fire**. These machines made known the miracles of the Demiurge, whose transparent image was illuminated by a **magical fire**; then he would reveal himself. These and other wonders were the designs of the **Magi** <note>original: "Magen"</note> and **master-sages**. Even in the fifth degree, people believed in these things, and one person always deceived the other.

At a certain time, they gathered in the temple in solemn attire; then the initiate appeared in the clothing of a penitent and confessed his crimes; then hymns were sung, the Demiurge bowed as a sign of forgiveness, the candidate was washed and sprinkled, and he received the sign of his rank along with his garments. Hymns were sung again, led by the **introducer** (the godfather) <note>original: "Pathe"</note> followed by the **confederate** <term>confederate</term> <note>original: "Bundesverwandte" — a fellow member or associate within the secret alliance.</note>. ### Chapter 4. Further Explanation.

The **Magi** <note>original: "Magen" — referring to the high-ranking masters or "wise men" of the order.</note> had especially studied the human heart, not theoretically but practically. A proof of this is the introduction of this confession <note>Referring to the requirement for initiates to confess their thoughts to their superiors mentioned on the previous page.</note>. For what was discovered through these confessions was used for political ends, even though it should not have been. The many miracles, which the priests allowed the **Demiurge** <note>The "artisan" of the world; here a statue or figure used in rituals to represent the creator.</note> to perform, won over all hearts; yet at their core, they were nothing but clever trickery. In the fifth degree, a person possessed much knowledge; but in the seventh, far more. The lesser associates of the covenant knew nothing of the secrets of the superiors. The holy mysteries were of very long duration, those of the Sages even longer; from time to time they merely changed names and some external forms. Moses was a Magus, although his history is an allegory; for example, the daughter of Pharaoh certainly did not bathe in the Nile—a river in which one never bathes due to the many crocodiles.

Out of political motives, the Knights Templar overthrew the Magical Covenant, and subsequently suffered a similar fate. In 1300, people began to burden them with accusations of vices, such as incest, the abduction of virgins, and **black magic**; yet their only true crime was their great wealth and their inclination toward freedom. Albert I, Philip IV (the Fair), and Clement V <note>The King of France and the Pope who historically orchestrated the dissolution of the Templars.</note> devised a plan to exterminate them; false witnesses were hired, and this shameful act of the Christians took place in 1306. And in 1311, the entire order was finally destroyed. The **Teutonic Order**, begun in the year 1191, initially had quite different intentions than those it later adopted. It shared certain core principles with the Knights Templar, which, however, could not be put into practice. Various other alliances continued to emerge until 1600, but they flickered out shortly after their creation. ### 3. Latest Collection of the Most Excellent Songs 
### for Brother Freemasons, Stendal: 
### Franzen and Grosse, 1782. Without index or 
### preface, 216 pages, octavo format.

The custom of <term>Freemasons</term><note>Members of a fraternal organization known for its rituals and use of architectural symbolism.</note> to sing certain songs appropriate to the occasion during their <term>table lodges</term><note>original: "Tafellogen"; formal ritualistic meals held by a Masonic lodge, characterized by toasts and singing.</note> has encouraged many poets to put their muse to work for this purpose. If one were to seek a similarity between this ritual and the <term>ancient mysteries</term><note>Secret religious cults of the Greco-Roman world, such as the Eleusinian Mysteries, which often involved initiation rites.</note>, one would be mistaken. To be sure, singing occurred there as well, but it consisted of hymns in praise of the <term>Demiurge</term><note>original: "Demiurgos"; in Gnosticism and Platonic philosophy, the artisan-like figure responsible for fashioning and maintaining the physical universe.</note>, not songs of cheerfulness for a company put in a joyful mood by food and wine—which, because it is certainly drunk in moderation, produces such high spirits. It is well known that songs are usually chosen which can be sung entirely, or for the most part, by a single brother [as a soloist], and consequently, a Freemason song ought to be a type of <term>round song</term><note>original: "Rundgesang"; a song sung by several people in succession or a communal song with a repeating refrain.</note>. We suspect that this book is already known to our readers, for the excellent prose style and the engaging quality that the French know how to impart to the subjects they wish to discuss—and in which the author, Abbé de Villars, <note>Henri de Montfaucon de Villars (1635–1673); his book "The Count of Gabalis" is a famous satire of Rosicrucianism and elemental spirits.</note> is in no way inferior to his countrymen—procures a multitude of readers who, in any case, seek to be amused rather than instructed. ### 5. Brotherly Admonitions to some Brother Freemasons by Brother Sedag. Philadelphia 1781. Octavo. 108 pages. <note>The imprint "Philadelphia" was frequently used as a false place of publication for controversial or Masonic books in the 18th century to evade local censorship.</note>

The intention, as the title indicates, is to direct certain Brother Freemasons not to cling to the outer shell, but to penetrate as far as possible into the inner core. Therefore, those who were admitted publicly could not know what was occurring within the inner circles of the Order; others remained silent about what they indeed knew. ### Section 3

Section 3 deals, therefore, with the individual accusations. The first concerns the **acquisition of property**, the oath sworn for that purpose, and their **breach of oath** against others. One cannot acquit them of the injustices proven by others in this regard. Secondly, they **absolved themselves** and believed that the **Grand Master** <term>Großmeister: the supreme head of the Knights Templar</term> could also release them from unconfessed sins. The superiors claimed that the **Pope** had granted them this power. If that accusation—along with the stubborn assertion that they believed themselves capable of releasing someone even from **excommunication** <note>original: "Bann"; the most severe ecclesiastical penalty, which excluded a person from the sacraments and the community of the Church</note>—is true, then the legal proceedings against them in that era are not surprising.

Thirdly, that they indulged in **illicit desires** is, for one, not so incredible, but is also substantiated by their own confession, in that they did not confess because of this sin and the shame of the flesh. Encountering a chivalric order in the thirteenth century that not only accepts such an important point contradicting the ruling Church but practices it in the greatest secrecy suggests—since in nature nothing happens **by a leap** <note>original: "per saltum"; a Latin philosophical principle suggesting that change occurs gradually rather than through sudden, disconnected jumps</note>—that the Order must have received teachings from somewhere from which such a practice naturally followed. The **unnatural vice** <note>original: "unnatürliche Unzucht"; a historical term used to refer to prohibited sexual acts, often sodomy</note> of which they were accused is, moreover, quite believable for their time, as even the most respected clergy had to clear themselves by oath to prove they were not in such a state.

This also applies, fourthly, to the **indecent kisses**, which could furthermore have served the purpose of deterring some from the Order through this kind of **hazing** <term>Hänseln: a term for mock-initiation or testing rituals, common in medieval guilds and secret societies, used to humble or challenge a newcomer</term> back...

### 12. Missive to the Sublime Unknown, or the True and Genuine Freemasons.

->You alone, only you know,<-
->How the eternal hand ever fashioned the earth and the sky,<-
->From the distinct chaos.<-
<note>original Italian: "Voi sol, sol voi sapete / Come mai fabricò la terra e' l cielo / Dal distinto cahos la mano eterna."</note>
->The clouded light shining over nature. Canto I.<-
<note>original Latin: "Lux obnub. s. nat. refulg. Cant. I." This refers to the alchemical poem *Lux obnubilata suapte natura refulgens*.</note>

1781. 200 octavo pages. With a neat Sphinx vignette.

The editor does not wish to be considered the same person as the author; he suggests that the author might perhaps be scolded as a <term>visionary</term> <note>original: "Schwärmer"; a derogatory 18th-century term for someone perceived as a religious or mystical fanatic.</note>, and yet he certainly is not—or if he were, the editor himself (which he does not believe) would have to conclude in a visionary manner. Doctors are said to expect a rather harsh lesson, and alchemists are also severely criticized; the editor claims he cannot be held responsible for this. The writing itself is distinguished from its "sisters" <note>Referring to other contemporary books on similar subjects.</note> by its style, which makes reading it tolerable; otherwise, it contains nothing new, for one is accustomed to the mocking laughter directed at thorough <term>natural research</term> <note>original: "Naturforschung"; the empirical study of the natural world.</note> and the <term>medical arts</term> <note>original: "Arzeneikunst"; the practice of medicine.</note>, especially coming from a certain class of people. The author pleads most earnestly that his "high superiors" might finally remove the blindfold from his eyes; admittedly, he has likely been seeing things very dimly.

<summary>This page contains a critical bibliographic review of a 1781 Masonic-alchemical publication, mocking its lack of original thought while noting its stylistic quality.</summary>
<keywords>Freemasonry, Alchemy, Bibliographic Review, Visionary (Schwärmer), Natural Research, Medical Arts, Sphinx Vignette, 18th Century Literature</keywords>
